q: Aurora Heights Apartment Tower is evaluating: (A) Install 400 kW of rooftop solar PV generating ~500,000 kWh/year; (B) Sign a 10-year PPA for 100% renewable electricity from a wind farm 200 miles away. Building annual electricity use is 2,000,000 kWh. Which strategy earns more LEED points?
options: On-site solar earns RE Production credit; off-site PPA earns Green Power — combine both
Both strategies earn identical LEED points since both involve renewable energy
Neither strategy earns LEED points since the building uses more electricity than the solar generates
Off-site PPAs always earn more LEED points than on-site solar
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: renewable energy: energy from sources that are naturally replenished; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; energy and atmosphere: strategies addressing energy demand, efficiency, refrigerants, and renewable energy
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: On-site solar earns RE Production credit; off-site PPA earns Green Power — combine both.
logic: LEED provides separate independent credits for on-site renewable energy and off-site green power. On-site generation typically earns more points per kWh because it provides permanent building improvements, resilience, and direct generation benefits. q: Crystal Tower Hotel has 450 guest rooms, a 200-seat restaurant, a rooftop pool, and cooling towers serving a 2,000-ton HVAC system. If the goal is to significantly reduce total water consumption, rank the conservation strategies by expected impact.

The pool should be addressed first since it is the most visible amenity
Cooling towers first (largest volume), then guest rooms, then kitchen, then pool
Start with low-flow showerheads in guest rooms since guests see them daily

vocabulary: cooling tower: heat-rejection equipment that commonly uses evaporation; water efficiency: reduction and responsible management of indoor, outdoor, and process water use; water performance: measured water consumption and the effectiveness of water-saving strategies
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Cooling towers first (largest volume), then guest rooms, then kitchen, then pool.
logic: Water conservation sequencing should prioritize by consumption volume. In hotels, cooling towers typically use 30–50% of total building water — more than all guest room fixtures combined. A single discharge event automatically fails the prerequisite
The discharge must be reported to GBCI within 24 hours or certification is lost
A single incident with immediate corrective action does not necessarily fail the prerequisite

vocabulary: construction activity pollution prevention: measures that prevent soil erosion, sedimentation, and construction-related pollution; erosion control: a measure that prevents soil from being detached and transported; prerequisite: a mandatory requirement that earns no points but is required for certification; certification: third-party confirmation that a project satisfies applicable LEED requirements
keywords: Choose the action that must occur early enough to influence subsequent project decisions; decisive action: A single incident with immediate corrective action does not necessarily fail the prerequisite.
logic: LEED's prerequisite is about implementing and maintaining a pollution prevention plan — not guaranteeing that no discharge ever occurs during extreme weather. Documentation showing the SWPPP was in place, the team immediately identified and corrected the failure, and reinforced controls demonstrates good faith compliance with the prerequisite intent.

The only solution is to install air curtain fume hoods to replace all existing hoods

vocabulary: best: a word asking for the strongest or most effective option; indoor environmental quality: conditions affecting indoor air, thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, and occupants; occupant health: health outcomes influenced by indoor environmental conditions
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: VAV fume hoods plus researcher training — better containment AND much less energy.
logic: This is a classic IAQ-energy nexus problem with an integrated solution. Lower sash heights actually IMPROVE chemical containment (better IAQ). Researcher training plus VAV controls simultaneously improves safety, IAQ, and energy.

q: Redwood Research Campus is demolishing a 1960s concrete laboratory with asbestos-containing materials (ACM) that must be abated before demolition. After proper abatement and clearance testing confirming the concrete rubble meets regulatory standards, can this concrete be counted toward C&D waste diversion?
options: Contaminated building materials cannot be recycled under any circumstances
All materials from asbestos-containing buildings must be landfilled for safety
Yes — properly abated and cleared concrete can be recycled and counted toward diversion
The abated concrete counts at 50% value since it was previously contaminated
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the MR concept and solve this sequence question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: waste diversion: keeping waste out of landfill or incineration through reuse, recycling, or recovery; best: a word asking for the strongest or most effective option; materials and resources: strategies addressing life-cycle impacts, product selection, sourcing, and waste
keywords: Choose the action that must occur early enough to influence subsequent project decisions; decisive action: Yes — properly abated and cleared concrete can be recycled and counted toward diversion.
logic: After proper abatement and clearance testing, the abated concrete can be crushed and recycled as aggregate — standard practice that counts toward C&D diversion. Required: ACM abatement by licensed contractor with documentation; clearance testing confirming the concrete is below ACM thresholds; recycling facility acceptance. The hazardous abatement waste itself does NOT count, but the cleared concrete does.

q: Cascade Heights Senior Center has a fitness center and woodworking hobby room. The designer has routed both spaces' HVAC exhaust back to the central air handling unit for heat recovery. The IAQ consultant flags this as a critical error. Why, and what is the correct solution?
options: The IAQ consultant is overreacting since the central AHU has MERV 13 filtration
Heat recovery from fitness centers is standard practice and there is no IAQ issue
Provide dedicated direct outdoor exhaust with air-to-air heat recovery — no recirculation
Heat recovery from woodworking shops is acceptable since wood dust is natural
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EQ concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: indoor environmental quality: conditions affecting indoor air, thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, and occupants; occupant health: health outcomes influenced by indoor environmental conditions
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Provide dedicated direct outdoor exhaust with air-to-air heat recovery — no recirculation.
logic: Recirculating exhaust from high-contaminant spaces (fitness CO₂/odors, woodshop dust/VOCs) through central air handling units is prohibited by ASHRAE 62.1 because it cross-contaminates all served spaces. MERV 13 filtration cannot remove CO₂, gaseous VOCs, humidity, or odors. The correct solution: dedicated direct exhaust outdoors with air-to-air heat exchangers that don't cross-contaminate.

The consultant is correct — LEED-ND certification replaces all LT documentation requirements
Architect partially right — LEED-ND earns one specific LT credit, not all of them
LEED-ND and LEED BD+C are mutually exclusive — a building cannot pursue both
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the PR concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; certification: third-party confirmation that a project satisfies applicable LEED requirements; documentation: records used to demonstrate compliance with a LEED requirement
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Architect partially right — LEED-ND earns one specific LT credit, not all of them.
logic: LEED-ND location earns a specific LEED BD+C credit (LEED Neighborhood Development Location) that represents significant point value. Yes — a previously developed site qualifies, and meadow restoration improves ecology

q: Riverside Office Complex is 0.8 miles from a commuter rail station. They propose a continuous shuttle with 10-minute headways during commute hours. How does this shuttle affect LEED Access to Quality Transit documentation?

q: Fairview Community Hospital wants to use extensive decorative exterior lighting for their patient-facing identity. The sustainability manager raises LEED Light Pollution Reduction concerns. The lighting designer argues decorative lighting is necessary. How should the team resolve this tension?
options: Specify decorative luminaires with proper BUG ratings — the credit doesn't ban decorative lighting
All exterior lighting must be turned off between dusk and dawn to earn the credit
The decorative lighting must be completely eliminated to earn the LEED credit
Healthcare facilities are exempt from Light Pollution Reduction requirements
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the SS concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; sustainable sites: strategies that protect site ecology and manage construction and operational site impacts; site disturbance: physical alteration of soil, vegetation, or existing site conditions
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Specify decorative luminaires with proper BUG ratings — the credit doesn't ban decorative lighting.
logic: LEED Light Pollution Reduction is about how light is directed (BUG ratings — backlight, uplight, glare), not eliminating all exterior lighting. Decorative lighting that illuminates the building facade with appropriate BUG-rated luminaires in warm color temperatures, pointed downward, and dimmed after 11 PM can earn the credit while meeting the hospital's image objectives.

q: Pinnacle Tower's whole-building LCA shows GWP contributors: Concrete structure (75,000 tonnes CO₂e), Steel reinforcement (12,000 tonnes), Aluminum curtain wall (8,500 tonnes), MEP systems (4,200 tonnes), Interior finishes (2,100 tonnes). Total: 101,800 tonnes. Reference building: 115,000 tonnes. What is the GWP reduction percentage, and which material offers the greatest opportunity for further improvement?
options: The total reduction is achieved — no further improvement is possible
The aluminum curtain wall should be the primary target for GWP reduction
A 11.5% reduction is too small to earn any LEED whole-building LCA credit
11.5% reduction — concrete (74% of GWP) is the biggest opportunity for further cuts
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the MR concept and solve this threshold question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; materials and resources: strategies addressing life-cycle impacts, product selection, sourcing, and waste; product documentation: verified records supporting environmental and material claims
keywords: Identify the exact minimum, maximum, or numerical threshold requested; decisive value or condition: 11.5% reduction — concrete (74% of GWP) is the biggest opportunity for further cuts.
logic: GWP reduction: (115,000 − 101,800) ÷ 115,000 = 11.5% — likely meeting the typical 10% LCA credit threshold. Concrete at 74% of total GWP is clearly the primary target for further improvement: a 40% SCM (fly ash/slag) replacement could reduce concrete GWP by 35–40%, potentially saving 26,000–30,000 tonnes CO₂e and pushing total reduction to 35%+.

q: Greenwood Elementary School is specifying interior materials: painted drywall walls, VCT flooring with adhesive, acoustical ceiling tiles, and solid wood casework. What is the most important product category to focus on for LEED Low-Emitting Materials compliance?
options: Only ceiling tiles matter since they are above occupant breathing height
Flooring system (VCT + adhesive) — highest VOC source close to children
All product categories are equally important and should be treated identically
Focus only on the paint since it is the most visible applied product
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the MR concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: low-emitting materials: products evaluated for low emissions of volatile organic compounds; materials and resources: strategies addressing life-cycle impacts, product selection, sourcing, and waste; product documentation: verified records supporting environmental and material claims
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Flooring system (VCT + adhesive) — highest VOC source close to children.
logic: Priority should be based on emission potential × exposure. Flooring adhesives are historically the highest VOC emitters in commercial interiors and are applied in confined spaces. Flooring covers large areas close to occupants — especially critical in schools where children are closest to the floor. Each component (adhesive, flooring, sealers) needs separate documentation.

q: Highpoint mixed-use development is in a water-stressed American Southwest region. The local utility offers a $3/1,000-gallon rebate for demonstrated water conservation. The team is evaluating: (A) native landscaping with no irrigation ($85,000 incremental cost), (B) WaterSense fixture upgrades ($45,000), (C) cooling tower optimization system ($35,000). Which investment likely provides the best combined return?
options: Option B because WaterSense fixtures are the most recognizable sustainable feature
Option C because cooling towers use the most water in all climates
All three options provide identical water savings and LEED credit value
Option A — landscape eliminates 60–70% of water use in arid climates
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the WE concept and solve this documentation question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: cooling tower: heat-rejection equipment that commonly uses evaporation; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; best: a word asking for the strongest or most effective option
keywords: Distinguish the technical requirement from the document or evidence that verifies it; decisive evidence: Option A — landscape eliminates 60–70% of water use in arid climates.
logic: Climate context is critical for water strategy prioritization. In the American Southwest, landscape irrigation typically represents 50–70% of total water use. Eliminating irrigation through native planting provides dramatically more total water savings than fixture upgrades, making it the highest-value strategy despite higher upfront cost.

q: Sunset Career Academy high school project includes a 600-seat auditorium, 40 classrooms, athletic facilities, and cafeteria. The acoustic consultant says 'LEED for Schools has one acoustic standard for all spaces.' The LEED coordinator knows this is incorrect. What is the accurate description of acoustic requirements across different space types?
options: Schools have space-type-specific acoustic requirements per ANSI/ASA S12.60 and others
Auditoriums and gymnasiums are exempt from LEED acoustic requirements
Only classrooms require acoustic compliance; all other school spaces are exempted
All spaces in schools require identical acoustic treatment under LEED
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EQ concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: indoor environmental quality: conditions affecting indoor air, thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, and occupants; occupant health: health outcomes influenced by indoor environmental conditions
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Schools have space-type-specific acoustic requirements per ANSI/ASA S12.60 and others.
logic: LEED for Schools' acoustic prerequisite and credits require space-type-appropriate acoustic performance. Classrooms target NC 35 max and specific reverberation times per ANSI/ASA S12.60 for speech intelligibility. Auditoriums, gymnasiums, and cafeterias each present entirely different acoustic challenges with different objectives — separate acoustic design is required.

q: Mapleview Elementary School's custodian has been using conventional janitorial products from the district's standard supply list — including bleach-based floor cleaner, petroleum-based furniture polish, and aerosol air fresheners. The principal notices occasional strong chemical odors and some student headaches. How does this relate to LEED's IEQ approach and what changes are needed?
options: Replace the HVAC filters since they must be clogged if odors are detectable
Janitorial products are outside LEED's scope once the building is occupied
Implement a green cleaning program with EPA Safer Choice products and eliminate aerosols
Increase ventilation rates to dilute the cleaning chemical odors
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EQ concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.

keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Implement a green cleaning program with EPA Safer Choice products and eliminate aerosols.
logic: Post-occupancy chemical management through green cleaning is as important as pre-occupancy low-emitting materials specification. A building designed with zero-VOC paints can have its IAQ degraded by conventional cleaning products (aerosol fresheners, petroleum polishes, bleach). For schools where children are vulnerable, EPA Safer Choice cleaning products and eliminating aerosols are essential.

q: Meridian Corporate Campus plans to install 1 MW of rooftop solar generating ~1,300,000 kWh/year. Building uses 5,000,000 kWh/year. The finance team wants to sell all the RECs generated for $0.05/REC = $65,000/year revenue. The LEED team objects. What is the LEED issue and how should it be resolved?
options: Selling RECs has no effect on LEED renewable energy credits
Selling RECs increases the LEED credit value since more money is invested in renewables
REC sales are irrelevant to LEED renewable energy credits in all circumstances
Selling RECs transfers the renewable attribute — building can't claim the RE Production credit
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: renewable energy: energy from sources that are naturally replenished; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; energy and atmosphere: strategies addressing energy demand, efficiency, refrigerants, and renewable energy
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Selling RECs transfers the renewable attribute — building can't claim the RE Production credit.
logic: RECs represent the renewable attribute of generated electricity. When sold, that attribute belongs to the buyer. A building that installs solar PV but sells all RECs has, from an accounting perspective, generated unclaimed renewable electricity — it cannot claim the LEED Renewable Energy Production credit for generation whose renewable attribute has been legally transferred away. Retain the RECs.

q: Solstice Energy Campus is tracking 54 points (Silver) and needs 6 more for Gold. The sustainability team proposes: (A) converting 1 acre of parking to bioretention prairie, (B) installing a green roof on 50% of the roof area, (C) upgrading all exterior lighting to dark-sky compliant LED. How much can the SS category contribute to closing this gap?
options: The SS strategies provide 0 points since the building is already past design
All three together could earn 5–7 SS points — sufficient to reach Gold
All three strategies together earn exactly 1 SS point
SS credits cannot be changed after the schematic design phase
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the SS concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: green roof: a vegetated roof assembly that can reduce runoff and heat gain; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; sustainable sites: strategies that protect site ecology and manage construction and operational site impacts
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: All three together could earn 5–7 SS points — sufficient to reach Gold.
logic: This case tests practical LEED strategy optimization: when close to a certification threshold, understanding the point value of each strategy enables targeted investment. Strategy A earns 3–4 points (Rainwater + Habitat + Open Space), Strategy B earns 1–2 (Heat Island), Strategy C earns 1 (Light Pollution) — collectively 5–7 SS points, enough to close the Silver-to-Gold gap.
